warmup.q: Quarkus's perf lab ran one service in JVM mode and as a native binary. The native binary answered its first request in 581 ms instead of 4,417 ms. What happened to its peak throughput?
options: It went up, because all the code was compiled ahead of time
It can't be measured, because native binaries have no JIT
warmup.why: Native peak throughput was 5,411 tps against 13,265 tps on the JVM. Ahead-of-time code is compiled without the run-time profiles the JIT uses, so it is less specialized. Native wins start-up and memory (95 MiB against 304 MiB RSS), not peak speed. Profile-guided optimization helps, but only in Oracle GraalVM.

sections.h: Native image builds a closed world
sections.html:
Lesson 2's AOT cache makes the JVM start faster, but it is still a JVM: it maps classes, links what training missed, interprets, and waits for the JIT. In Quarkus's benchmark below, the first request still took 1,859 ms with the cache. Native image removes that work from the start by doing it all in the build.

native-image, from GraalVM or from Mandrel (the distribution "tailored for Quarkus"), takes your class path and builds one executable for one OS and CPU, in three steps. First it analyzes: starting at main, it follows every method call and field access it can see, and works out which classes can show up at each call. Second it runs static initializers where it can, and saves the objects they created into the image heap, a section of the executable that is mapped into memory at start-up. Third it compiles every reachable method to machine code. Code the analysis never reached is left out, and so are the JDK classes nothing uses. This is the closed-world assumption: everything the program will ever run is known when you build it.

The binary runs on a small runtime, SubstrateVM, with no class loading, no bytecode verification, no interpreter and no JIT. That is why it starts fast and stays small. The Quarkus docs publish a tuned benchmark (Quarkus 3.34.3, JDK 25.0.2):

JVM JVM + AOT cache Native (Mandrel)
Time to first request 4,417 ms 1,859 ms 581 ms
Peak throughput 13,265 tps 12,389 tps 5,411 tps
RSS 304 MiB 240 MiB 95 MiB
Build about 30 s build plus a training run 3 to 10 min, 4 to 8 GB of RAM

Peak throughput is 59% lower. With no JIT there are no run-time profiles, and GraalVM's own docs say that "without profiling information, it is difficult to generate machine code of the same quality as a JIT compiler". Profile-guided optimization (PGO: building again with profiles recorded from a test run) narrows the gap, but "PGO is not available in GraalVM Community Edition". The default garbage collector is Serial, a single-threaded collector "optimized for low footprint and small Java heap sizes"; G1 is available only in Oracle GraalVM, on Linux.

The other price is everything the analysis can't see: reflection, dynamic proxies, resources loaded by name, JNI (calls into native C code) and serialization. The analysis copes with constants. GraalVM works out reflective calls at build time "given that all the call arguments are constant", so Class.forName("com.acme.pay.Fees") with a literal just works. Class.forName(record.headers().get("type")) does not: the class name arrives with the Kafka message, and the build can't know it. You have to tell the build, or the call fails at run time. Current GraalVM throws MissingReflectionRegistrationError, which "extends java.lang.Error and should not be handled".

try.title: A class name that only exists at run time
steps: Read DynamicLookupDemo. It calls a static no-argument method chosen by two strings.
Run it as is, then with -Pargs='java.util.UUID randomUUID'. Any class on the class path works on the JVM.
Ask yourself which classes a build would have to keep to support every possible argument. That is why the build needs a list.

Optional, needs a GraalVM JDK: run the class with java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=build/ni -cp startup/build/classes/java/demo workbench.startup.l03.demo.DynamicLookupDemo java.util.UUID randomUUID and look at the JSON the agent wrote into build/ni.

code.title: DynamicLookupDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Method; /** * Calls a static, no-argument method chosen at run time, by class name and method name. * On the JVM any class on the class path works. A native image can only do this for the * classes and methods listed in its reachability metadata, so the demo prints that entry too. */ public class DynamicLookupDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String className = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "java.time.LocalDate"; String methodName = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "now"; Class<?> type = Class.forName(className); // a name from data: the analysis can't see it Method method = type.getMethod(methodName); System.out.println(className + "." + methodName + "() = " + method.invoke(null)); System.out.println("A native image needs this in reachability-metadata.json:"); System.out.printf("{ \"reflection\": [ { \"type\": \"%s\", \"methods\": [ { \"name\": \"%s\", \"parameterTypes\": [] } ] } ] }%n", type.getName(), method.getName()); } }

alt.title: DynamicLookupDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo /** * Calls a static, no-argument method chosen at run time, by class name and method name. * On the JVM any class on the class path works. A native image can only do this for the * classes and methods listed in its reachability metadata, so the demo prints that entry too. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val className = args.getOrElse(0) { "java.time.LocalDate" } val methodName = args.getOrElse(1) { "now" } val type = Class.forName(className) // a name from data: the analysis can't see it val method = type.getMethod(methodName) println("$className.$methodName() = ${method.invoke(null)}") println("A native image needs this in reachability-metadata.json:") println("""{ "reflection": [ { "type": "${type.name}", "methods": [ { "name": "${method.name}", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] }""") }

try.expect: The first run prints today's date and the entry { "type": "java.time.LocalDate", "methods": [ { "name": "now", "parameterTypes": [] } ] }. The second prints a random UUID and an entry for java.util.UUID and randomUUID. On the JVM both just work. A native image would work only for the class and method its metadata listed.

sections.h: Reflection and proxies need reachability metadata
sections.html:
You tell the build in reachability-metadata.json, placed in META-INF/native-image/<groupId>/<artifactId>/ on the class path. The current schema is v1.2.0, and its top level has four keys: reflection, resources, foreign and comment. Proxies, serialization and JNI all live inside reflection entries.

A reflection entry names a type and the members your code uses:

{
  "reflection": [
    {
      "condition": { "typeReached": "com.acme.pay.EventDecoder" },
      "type": "com.acme.pay.PaymentAuthorized",
      "methods": [
        { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] },
        { "name": "paymentId", "parameterTypes": [] }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

A constructor is called <init>. Parameter types are fully qualified, primitives by name (long, int), and every method needs parameterTypes, even an empty one. Instead of listing members you can set allDeclaredConstructors or allPublicMethods, which keeps more code in the binary. The optional condition switches the entry on only once EventDecoder is reached at run time, which means just before its initializer starts; EventDecoder.class on its own doesn't count.

A JDK dynamic proxy is a reflection entry whose type is an ordered list of interfaces:

{ "reflection": [ { "type": { "proxy": ["com.acme.pay.CardIssuerClient", "java.lang.AutoCloseable"] } } ] }

The order is part of the proxy's identity: a proxy for (A, B) is a different class from one for (B, A). If the proxy gets serialized, add "serializable": true; the docs say proxies "can only be registered for serialization via the JSON files".

Two warnings about documentation. The older schema, v1.1.0, had separate top-level jni and serialization sections, and some GraalVM prose still shows a top-level jni array; v1.2.0 rejects it. The current Quarkus main-branch docs say to use "a proxy section", which v1.2.0 also rejects. Check your file against the schema of the GraalVM you build with.

You rarely write all of it by hand. The tracing agent watches a run on a normal JVM and writes what it saw: java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=build/ni-config -jar app.jar. Like an AOT training run, it only sees the code paths you exercise, so drive it with your integration tests and then read what it wrote. To make gaps fail loudly, build with --exact-reachability-metadata and run the tests with -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit.

try.title: The order of proxy interfaces
steps: Read ProxyOrderDemo. It builds three proxies: (IssuerApi, AutoCloseable), (AutoCloseable, IssuerApi), and the first pair again.
Predict the two same class lines before you run it.
Run it, then the Kotlin twin.

code.title: ProxyOrderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.Arrays; /** Builds two JDK dynamic proxies from the same two interfaces, in opposite orders. */ public class ProxyOrderDemo { public interface IssuerApi { String authorize(String paymentId); } public static void main(String[] args) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, a) -> method.getName().equals("authorize") ? "APPROVED " + a[0] : null; ClassLoader loader = ProxyOrderDemo.class.getClassLoader(); Object first = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {IssuerApi.class, AutoCloseable.class}, handler); Object second = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {AutoCloseable.class, IssuerApi.class}, handler); Object again = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {IssuerApi.class, AutoCloseable.class}, handler); System.out.println("first : " + first.getClass().getName() + " " + names(first.getClass())); System.out.println("second: " + second.getClass().getName() + " " + names(second.getClass())); System.out.println("same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? " + (first.getClass() == second.getClass())); System.out.println("same class for (A, B) twice? " + (first.getClass() == again.getClass())); System.out.println(((IssuerApi) first).authorize("pay_81")); } static String names(Class<?> c) { return Arrays.toString(Arrays.stream(c.getInterfaces()).map(Class::getSimpleName).toArray()); } }

alt.title: ProxyOrderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler import java.lang.reflect.Proxy /** Builds two JDK dynamic proxies from the same two interfaces, in opposite orders. */ interface IssuerApi { fun authorize(paymentId: String): String } fun main() { val handler = InvocationHandler { _, method, a -> if (method.name == "authorize") "APPROVED ${a[0]}" else null } val loader = IssuerApi::class.java.classLoader val first = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(IssuerApi::class.java, AutoCloseable::class.java), handler) val second = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(AutoCloseable::class.java, IssuerApi::class.java), handler) val again = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(IssuerApi::class.java, AutoCloseable::class.java), handler) fun names(c: Class<*>) = c.interfaces.map { it.simpleName } println("first : ${first.javaClass.name} ${names(first.javaClass)}") println("second: ${second.javaClass.name} ${names(second.javaClass)}") println("same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? ${first.javaClass == second.javaClass}") println("same class for (A, B) twice? ${first.javaClass == again.javaClass}") println((first as IssuerApi).authorize("pay_81")) }

try.expect: The first two proxies are different classes, jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0 and jdk.proxy1.$Proxy1, so same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? prints false. The repeat of the first pair reuses $Proxy0 and prints true. The JVM caches one proxy class per ordered interface list, which is why the metadata lists interfaces in order.

sections.h: The build is your program's first run
sections.html:
Class initialization is the other half of the story. GraalVM's docs give the numbers: "the simple 'Hello, World!' application requires more than 300 classes to be initialized", and in code compiled ahead of time, the check "is this class initialized yet?" on every access "can reduce performance by more than twofold". So the builder runs static initializers at build time where it can, and stores what they produced in the image heap.

Plain GraalVM initializes most JDK classes at build time, and your classes only when it can prove that safe. An initializer that calls native code (System.out.println counts), makes a virtual call it can't pin to one target, or reaches a substituted method stays at run time. Quarkus goes further: "By default, Quarkus initializes all classes at build time."

So your static initializer runs on the build machine, once, and its results are frozen into the binary:

Java
static final Instant STARTED_AT = Instant.now();   // the build's time, on every start
static final Random JITTER = new Random();         // the builder refuses this one
Kotlin
val startedAt: Instant = Instant.now()             // the build's time, on every start
val jitter = Random()                              // the builder refuses this one

The builder catches some of these. Quarkus lists two errors you are likely to meet: "Detected an instance of Random/SplittableRandom class in the image heap. Instances created during image generation have cached seed values", and "No instances are allowed in the image heap for a class that is initialized or reinitialized at image runtime: sun.security.provider.NativePRNG". Don't count on it for the rest. A timestamp, a hostname, a token fetched at start: whatever an initializer computes, every container started from that image sees the value from the build.

The fix is to initialize that class at run time:

quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-run-time=com.acme.pay.InstanceInfo\\,com.acme.pay.RetryJitter

Quarkus needs the comma escaped. With plain native-image the options are --initialize-at-run-time= and --initialize-at-build-time=, and -H:+PrintClassInitialization reports what was initialized where. Better still, keep per-instance values out of static initializers, and compute them in a method that runs at start-up.

try.title: Values that would be frozen at build time
steps: Read BuildTimeInitDemo. Two static fields are set in a class initializer.
Run it twice and compare the output of the two runs.
Now imagine the class was initialized at build time, the Quarkus default. Which line would be the same on every start of every pod, and which one would stop the build?

code.title: BuildTimeInitDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.time.Instant; import java.util.Random; /** * Static state computed in a class initializer. On the JVM it is computed again on every start. * In a native image built with build-time initialization (the Quarkus default), the initializer * runs once, inside the build, and every start of the binary sees the build's values. */ public class BuildTimeInitDemo { static final class InstanceInfo { static final Instant STARTED_AT = Instant.now(); // build-time init: the build's time, forever static final Random JITTER = new Random(); // build-time init: the native builder rejects it } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("started at: " + InstanceInfo.STARTED_AT); System.out.println("retry jitter ms: " + InstanceInfo.JITTER.nextInt(250)); } }

alt.title: BuildTimeInitDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo import java.time.Instant import java.util.Random /** * Static state computed in a class initializer. On the JVM it is computed again on every start. * In a native image built with build-time initialization (the Quarkus default), the initializer * runs once, inside the build, and every start of the binary sees the build's values. */ object InstanceInfo { val startedAt: Instant = Instant.now() // build-time init: the build's time, forever val jitter = Random() // build-time init: the native builder rejects it } fun main() { println("started at: ${InstanceInfo.startedAt}") println("retry jitter ms: ${InstanceInfo.jitter.nextInt(250)}") }

try.expect: On the JVM each run prints a new started at time and a new jitter value, because the initializer runs at every start. Initialized at build time, started at would print the build's timestamp forever, in every container. The Random in the image heap is one of the cases the builder refuses, with the "cached seed values" error.

refs.title: GraalVM: Class Initialization in Native Image

sections.h: Quarkus writes most of the metadata for you
sections.html:
In a Quarkus app you rarely touch the JSON. Quarkus extensions know what their libraries reflect on, and Quarkus generates reachability-metadata.json itself. Your part is the classes only your code knows about, and annotations are the way to declare them:

Java
@RegisterForReflection
public record PaymentAuthorized(String paymentId, String currency, long amountMinor) { }

@RegisterForReflection(targets = {IssuerResponse.class, IssuerError.class})   // a library's classes
public class IssuerReflectionConfig { }

@RegisterForProxy(targets = {CardIssuerClient.class, AutoCloseable.class})    // order matters
public class IssuerProxyConfig { }
Kotlin
@RegisterForReflection
data class PaymentAuthorized(val paymentId: String, val currency: String, val amountMinor: Long)

@RegisterForReflection(targets = [IssuerResponse::class, IssuerError::class])  // a library's classes
class IssuerReflectionConfig

@RegisterForProxy(targets = [CardIssuerClient::class, AutoCloseable::class])   // order matters
class IssuerProxyConfig

@RegisterForReflection registers methods and fields by default, plus any nested classes unless you set ignoreNested = true. With targets it registers the listed classes and not the class it sits on, which is how you cover a library's classes that you can't annotate. serialization = true adds Java serialization. @RegisterForProxy takes the interfaces in order, and the Quarkus docs repeat that "the order of the specified proxy interfaces is significant". Resources go in application.properties: quarkus.native.resources.includes=templates/**,rates/*.csv.

When you do need JSON, put it in src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/<group-id>/<artifact-id>/; the current docs warn that Quarkus overwrites a file placed directly in META-INF/native-image/. The Quarkus 3.x guides still show the older separate files, reflect-config.json and proxy-config.json, while the 4.0 guides say those legacy files "are not supported". Write the unified reachability-metadata.json and the file survives the upgrade.

./mvnw verify -Dnative builds the binary and runs your @QuarkusIntegrationTests against it. Because a native build takes minutes and gigabytes, most teams run it in CI and develop in JVM mode. Quarkus's own advice is "Start with JVM mode. Move to native when you have a concrete need." Lesson 4 of this track turns that into a decision table.

Check before the lab: your event classes live in a shared payment-events JAR that another team owns, so you can't annotate them. Which annotation do you add, and on which class? (@RegisterForReflection(targets = {...}) on any class in your own code, listing their classes; the class carrying the annotation is not registered itself.)

refs.title: Quarkus 3.40: Tips for writing native applications

analogy: A JVM is a library with every book on the shelves: you can ask for any title, at any time. A native image is a printed booklet with only the pages someone proved you will read, bound in one cover. It is thin and opens instantly. But if your code looks up a page by a name that arrives in a message, the page has to be on the list you gave the printer, or it isn't in the booklet. Build-time initialization is the printer filling in the blanks on some pages before binding, so a date written there is the printing date. The analogy breaks on speed: a booklet is read faster than a library is searched, but a native binary runs hot code slower than a warmed JVM, because no one rewrites the pages after watching how you read.
world: A Kafka consumer in a payments service is the classic native trap: the deserializer picks the event class from a header, Jackson creates it and calls its accessors by reflection, and a REST client to the card issuer is a dynamic proxy. In Quarkus the extensions register what they know about, and you add @RegisterForReflection to your event classes, or targets = [...] for event classes from a shared schema library you can't annotate. Look for static state that must differ per pod: an instance id for idempotency keys, a start timestamp in health output, a SecureRandom for nonces. Under build-time initialization they'd be the same in every pod, and some won't even build. Native pays off for scale-to-zero functions and for packing many small services on a node. For a consumer that runs all day at high throughput, the 59% lower peak in Quarkus's benchmark is usually the deciding number.
mistake: The usual mistake is copying a metadata snippet from an old blog post or from a different GraalVM version and trusting it. A top-level "proxy" or "jni" array, or a reflect-config.json dropped into a Quarkus 4 project, either fails schema v1.2.0 or is ignored, and the proxy or class it was meant to cover fails at run time in the one code path your smoke test didn't hit. Write proxies as reflection entries with "type": {"proxy": [...]}, prefer @RegisterForReflection and @RegisterForProxy in Quarkus, and run the native integration tests with -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit so a gap fails the build instead of a payment.

compare.title: The same event class registered from Java and from Kotlin

java.title: PaymentAuthorized.java
java.html: @RegisterForReflection public record PaymentAuthorized(String paymentId, String currency, long amountMinor) { } // the same thing by hand in reachability-metadata.json: // { "type": "com.acme.pay.PaymentAuthorized", // "methods": [ // { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, // { "name": "paymentId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] }

kotlin.title: PaymentAuthorized.kt
kotlin.html: @RegisterForReflection data class PaymentAuthorized(val paymentId: String, val currency: String, val amountMinor: Long) // the same thing by hand: the accessor is a getter on the JVM // { "type": "com.acme.pay.PaymentAuthorized", // "methods": [ // { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, // { "name": "getPaymentId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] }

compare.note: The annotation is the same, and Quarkus reads it the same way from both languages. What differs is the bytecode it describes. A Java record has an accessor named paymentId(). A Kotlin val paymentId compiles to a private field and a method named getPaymentId(). Hand-written metadata names JVM members, so the two entries differ even though the sources look alike. A non-null Kotlin Long is the primitive long in the constructor's signature; Long? would be java.lang.Long. Annotation arrays are {...} with .class in Java and [...] with ::class in Kotlin.

worked.title: Write the metadata for a Kafka event decoder

steps.say: Here is the decoder. Find every reflective call and, for each, the exact member it needs. Ignore code that uses classes by name in source, such as new or a direct method call: the analysis sees those.
steps.code: Object decode(ConsumerRecord<String, String> rec) throws ReflectiveOperationException { Class<?> type = Class.forName(new String(rec.headers().lastHeader("type").value())); // 1 Object event = type.getConstructor(String.class, String.class, long.class) // 2 .newInstance(rec.key(), currencyOf(rec), amountOf(rec)); audit.log(type.getMethod("paymentId").invoke(event)); // 3 return event; }

alt.html: fun decode(rec: ConsumerRecord<String, String>): Any { val type = Class.forName(String(rec.headers().lastHeader("type").value())) // 1 val event = type.getConstructor(String::class.java, String::class.java, Long::class.javaPrimitiveType) // 2 .newInstance(rec.key(), currencyOf(rec), amountOf(rec)) audit.log(type.getMethod("paymentId").invoke(event)) // 3 return event }

steps.say: Three needs: (1) the class by name, for every event type the topic can carry; (2) its (String, String, long) constructor; (3) its paymentId() method. Say the topic carries PaymentAuthorized and PaymentCaptured. Each gets one entry. The condition limits them to images where the decoder is used.
steps.code: { "reflection": [ { "condition": { "typeReached": "com.acme.pay.EventDecoder" }, "type": "com.acme.pay.PaymentAuthorized", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, { "name": "paymentId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] }, { "condition": { "typeReached": "com.acme.pay.EventDecoder" }, "type": "com.acme.pay.PaymentCaptured", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, { "name": "paymentId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] }

steps.say: Put the file at src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/com.acme/pay-events/reachability-metadata.json, the <groupId>/<artifactId> folder. In a Quarkus app, the annotation does the same job and moves with the class when someone renames it. That is the version to prefer.
steps.code: @RegisterForReflection public record PaymentAuthorized(String paymentId, String currency, long amountMinor) { } @RegisterForReflection public record PaymentCaptured(String paymentId, String currency, long amountMinor) { }

alt.html: @RegisterForReflection data class PaymentAuthorized(val paymentId: String, val currency: String, val amountMinor: Long) @RegisterForReflection data class PaymentCaptured(val paymentId: String, val currency: String, val amountMinor: Long)

steps.say: Prove it in CI. Build the native binary and run the integration tests against it with missing registrations turned into a hard exit. A new event type that nobody registered now fails the pipeline, not a refund at 3 a.m.
steps.code: ./mvnw verify -Dnative \ -Dquarkus.native.additional-build-args=--exact-reachability-metadata # and start the binary under test with -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit

lab.title: Write reachability metadata for a class and a proxy
steps: Run the tests once. Eight of ten fail. Two MetadataFileTest checks pass already: the empty stub file has a valid shape.
Read EventDecoder and IssuerClients. Write down every reflective call: which class, which constructor (with its parameter types), which methods, and which proxy interfaces in which order.

Edit reachability-metadata.json by hand. Add one reflection entry for workbench.startup.l03.PaymentAuthorized with its <init> and the three accessors from EventDecoder.ACCESSORS, and one entry whose type is {"proxy": [...]}. Run MetadataFileTest until it passes.
Implement MetadataWriter.reflection and MetadataWriter.proxy, so the same entries can be generated from Class objects. Run all ten tests.
hints: A method entry needs both keys, even with no parameters: {"name": "currency", "parameterTypes": []}.
Class.getName() gives exactly the names the schema wants: java.lang.String for a class, long for a primitive.
m instanceof Constructor<?> tells a constructor from a method. Class.isInterface() and a HashSet cover the two proxy rules.
lab.done: All ten tests in MetadataFileTest and MetadataWriterTest pass.

drill.title: Two entries from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a reachability-metadata.json that registers (1) a JDK proxy over com.acme.ledger.LedgerClient and java.io.Closeable, in that order, and (2) the (java.lang.String, long) constructor of com.acme.ledger.Refund, active only when com.acme.ledger.RefundListener is reached. Check: how many top-level keys did you use?

answer.html: { "reflection": [ { "type": { "proxy": ["com.acme.ledger.LedgerClient", "java.io.Closeable"] } }, { "condition": { "typeReached": "com.acme.ledger.RefundListener" }, "type": "com.acme.ledger.Refund", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "long"] } ] } ] }

recap: Native image analyzes from main at build time and keeps only reachable code: fast start and small RSS, but no JIT, so lower peak throughput (59% lower in Quarkus's benchmark), and builds that take minutes and gigabytes.
Whatever the analysis can't see (reflection by a run-time name, proxies, resources, JNI, serialization) must be declared in META-INF/native-image/<groupId>/<artifactId>/reachability-metadata.json.
Schema v1.2.0 has only reflection, resources, foreign and comment at the top. A proxy is a reflection entry with "type": {"proxy": [interfaces in order]}; constructors are <init>.

Quarkus initializes all classes at build time by default: static initializers run on the build machine and their values are frozen into the binary. Use --initialize-at-run-time for classes that must run at start.
In Quarkus prefer @RegisterForReflection (with targets for library classes) and @RegisterForProxy over hand-written JSON, and test the native binary in CI.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why a native image needs metadata for the event class your Kafka deserializer creates by reflection, but not for a class your code creates with new, and what Quarkus gives you so you don't write the JSON by hand.
explain.answer: The native build analyzes the program from main and keeps only code it can prove is reachable. A new PaymentAuthorized(...) is right there in the bytecode, so the analysis sees the class and its constructor. The deserializer instead calls Class.forName with a name from the message header and then getConstructor and getMethod, so the build can't know which class or which members until the message arrives. Unless the class and those members are listed in reachability metadata, they're left out, and the call fails at run time with a registration error. In Quarkus, the extensions register what their libraries need, and I add @RegisterForReflection to my event classes, or use targets for classes from a library, and @RegisterForProxy for proxies. Quarkus turns those into the metadata file during the build.

deeper.html:
Some details for when you go native for real.

Conditions are precise. "condition": {"typeReached": "com.acme.EventDecoder"} makes an entry active when that type is reached at run time, which the docs define as "right before the class-initialization routine starts for that type", or when one of its subtypes is reached. Writing EventDecoder.class does not reach it. Conditions mostly help library authors ship metadata that costs nothing in apps that never use the feature.

Resources use globs: {"resources": [{"glob": "META-INF/**/*.properties"}, {"bundle": "com.acme.Messages"}]}. In Quarkus, use quarkus.native.resources.includes instead.

The heap needs a limit. Without an explicit maximum, a native image sets the maximum Java heap to 80% of the physical memory size, according to the GraalVM memory docs. In a container, pass -Xmx (or -XX:MaximumHeapSizePercent) yourself. The default collector is Serial. --gc=G1 needs Oracle GraalVM on Linux, and --gc=epsilon never frees memory, which only makes sense for short jobs.

PGO, in Oracle GraalVM only, is a three-step build: native-image --pgo-instrument ... builds an instrumented binary, you run it on a real workload so it writes a .iprof profile on exit, and native-image --pgo=app.iprof ... builds the optimized binary. That is the same idea as Leyden's training run, applied to compiled code.

The JDK is moving toward some of these benefits without leaving the JVM. Lesson 2's AOT cache already ships linked classes and profiles, and JEP 544, in development for JDK 28, adds compiled code to the cache while keeping the JIT. Native image stays the option when the binary's size and start time, not the JVM's, are the limit.
